For a natural-disaster trauma, 'People cycling' is a hard-to-explain trigger unless there is disaster-specific context, which is not supported by the rest of the profile. The other items do not provide a plausible link to bicycles/cyclists.
'Being alone with men' implies an interpersonal/assault-related trigger context that is not reflected in the trauma type or elsewhere in the profile, making it clinically incoherent here.

Avoidance of unfamiliar places due to inability to assess danger can occur in PTSD, but alongside the selected triggers it pulls toward an interpersonal/urban threat pattern rather than a natural-disaster pattern. This becomes problematic because the threat items are not meaningfully linked to the disaster-specific cues represented elsewhere.

vignette: When the coastal storm surge breached the sea wall, Tane and his wife were trapped in the lower hallway as water roared through the cracked windows. He remembers the thick, metallic taste of brine flooding his mouth and the acrid smell of uprooted mangrove choking the air. The violence of the current was so absolute that days later he would sit at his kitchen table and struggle to accept that the story was real, as if the trauma had somehow detached from his own life. In the months that followed, ordinary moments rapidly became dangerous signals. When his team shared a laugh at a client lunch, the sudden spike of happiness felt like a warning bell, instantly pulling back the flood’s taste and smell. Because feeling relaxed made him fear he was letting his guard down, he turned to smoking two packs a day, refused to sit through a single unstructured hour without a ledger in front of him, and stopped talking with his colleagues about the event or its aftermath. These coping habits did not contain the fear; instead, they cemented his conviction that he was powerless to stop catastrophe, that the world was fundamentally unsafe, and that he was emotionally dead inside. This fractured appraisal system then amplified his threat monitoring. His conviction that he was helpless and the world was dangerous directly caused him to refuse relaxation and avoid talking about the event, treating conversation as a liability. Because he believed the world was dangerous and he could not control it, he began avoiding unfamiliar physical locations, convinced he could never adequately scan for hidden risks. In his new office, when a supplier delay stretched past the expected hour, he would assume something terrible was imminent. His belief that he was emotionally dead inside made the memories feel fragmented and detached, as if the story were unreal. His conviction that he was helpless also made ordinary moments like feeling happy or waking in the dark feel suddenly treacherous, amplifying his sensitivity to those cues. When his team shared a laugh, the sudden spike of happiness felt like a warning bell, instantly pulling back the flood’s taste and smell, which in turn made him braced for disaster. This sensitivity to sudden joy meant that spatial cues and the dark immediately activated his threat response, making him hyperaware of every threshold and hallway. The persistent recall of the event’s sensory details would make him acutely aware of every doorway and corridor, turning routine spaces into immediate triggers. Even unusual quiet in the breakroom would make him braced for disaster, and that sudden fixation on silence would directly pull the olfactory memory of decaying wetwood back into his conscious mind. When the memory returned, it immediately flared his threat response, making him braced for impact. His avoidance strategies quickly rewired his daily reality. By refusing to relax and constantly smoking to manage his anxiety, he inadvertently trained his nervous system to remain on high alert, making the triggers of nighttime darkness and sudden joy feel more invasive and unmanageable. This avoidance of processing the disaster left no room for reality-testing, so the threat of delays in audit files grew into a paralyzing certainty that catastrophe was always around the corner, which further reinforced his belief that he was helpless and emotionally numb. Over months, his isolation became concrete. He stopped taking site auditors out for meals, claiming tight deadlines, and declined his mother-in-law’s invitations to visit, telling himself that unfamiliar territory was simply too risky to navigate. His work suffered when he abruptly canceled a regional inspection after a simple supply delay, citing a sudden need for "extra caution," which drew sharp emails from his partners and threatened his standing at the firm. Tane finally sought help when a routine nighttime audit pulled him to the office at 2 a.m., and the sudden stillness of the empty floor made his heart hammer with the same certainty that the flood was returning. He no longer wants to wake up braced for impact or feel dead inside while his colleagues plan their next moves. He is hoping to find a way to sit with his grief without it feeling like a threat, and to walk through physical spaces without expecting the floor to give way.
